promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: What the gold-foil scattering experiment showed and why a nucleus follows
Reading and writing nuclide notation: A, Z and isotopes
How line spectra show that atomic energy levels are discrete
Finding the photon's frequency and wavelength from the gap between levels
Using spectra to tell which elements are present
Mass defect and binding energy
Using E = mc² in nuclear reactions and decays
The strong nuclear force: short-range and attractive
How α, β and γ emission change the nucleus
Writing balanced decay equations for α, β⁻, β⁺ and γ
Neutrinos and antineutrinos exist
Penetration and ionizing power of α, β and γ, and choosing an isotope

questions.q: Which statement about the results of the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford alpha-particle scattering experiment is correct?
options: Most of the alpha particles were deflected through large angles, and only a few passed straight through.
Nearly all the alpha particles passed through almost undeflected; a very few were deflected by more than 90°.
The few alpha particles that bounced back had collided with the electrons in the gold atoms.
The few alpha particles that bounced back had struck the hard outer surface of a gold nucleus.
optionWhy: A student who remembers the dramatic rebounds as the main result picks this. The reverse happened: nearly all passed through with little or no deflection, and large deflections were very rare.

Almost every alpha particle went through the thin gold foil almost undeflected, and a very small fraction were deflected through large angles, some through more than 90°. Both parts matter: the rarity shows the nucleus is tiny, and the large deflections show its charge and mass are concentrated.

A student who pictures electrons as the particles an alpha particle can hit picks this. An electron has about 1/7300 of an alpha particle's mass, so it cannot turn one back; only the massive, positive nucleus can.

A student who thinks a deflection needs contact picks this. The alpha particles were turned back by electric repulsion, which acts at a distance; they stopped and reversed before reaching the nucleus.
questions.explain: Almost every alpha particle went through the thin gold foil almost undeflected, and a very small fraction were deflected through large angles, some through more than 90°. Both parts matter: the rarity shows the nucleus is tiny, and the large deflections show its charge and mass are concentrated.
questions.working: No calculation is needed. The results: almost all alpha particles passed through the foil with little or no deflection; a very small fraction were deflected through large angles, some through more than 90°.

questions.q: A nucleus of potassium-40 is written in nuclear notation as ⁴⁰₁₉K. Which statement about this nucleus is correct?
options: It contains 40 neutrons.
It contains 19 neutrons.
It contains 19 nucleons.
It contains 21 neutrons.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the nucleon number counts only neutrons picks this. A = 40 counts protons and neutrons together; the neutrons number 40 − 19 = 21.
A student who assumes a nucleus always has equal numbers of protons and neutrons picks this. That holds only for some light nuclei; here N = 40 − 19 = 21.
A student who reads the lower number as the nucleon number picks this. In nuclear notation the lower number is the proton number; the nucleon number is the upper number, 40.
In ᴬ_Z X the upper number is the nucleon number A = 40 and the lower number is the proton number Z = 19, so the number of neutrons is N = A − Z = 40 − 19 = 21.
questions.explain: In ᴬ_Z X the upper number is the nucleon number A = 40 and the lower number is the proton number Z = 19, so the number of neutrons is N = A − Z = 40 − 19 = 21.
questions.working: A = 40 (upper number), Z = 19 (lower number). Protons = 19; nucleons = 40; neutrons N = A − Z = 40 − 19 = 21.

questions.q: The emission spectrum of a hot, low-pressure gas of one element consists of bright lines at a set of separate wavelengths. Why is this evidence that the atoms have discrete energy levels?
options: Each line has the photon energy of one allowed level, so each line marks one energy level.
The lines are equally spaced in frequency, just as the atom's energy levels are equally spaced.
Each line is emitted as an electron jumps up from one allowed level to a higher level.
Each line has a single photon energy, equal to the difference between two of the atom's allowed energies.
optionWhy: A student who links one line to one level picks this. A photon's energy equals the difference between two levels, so each line marks a pair of levels, and there can be more lines than levels.
A student who pictures energy levels as evenly spaced rungs picks this. Spectral lines are not equally spaced, and neither are the levels; in hydrogen they crowd together at higher energies.
A student who links emission with excitation picks this. Moving up needs energy; a photon is emitted when the electron moves down, and the line's photon energy is the energy lost.

Each line contains photons of one frequency and therefore one energy, E = hf. A fixed set of photon energies means the atom can change its energy only by fixed amounts, the differences between a fixed set of allowed levels.
questions.explain: Each line contains photons of one frequency and therefore one energy, E = hf. A fixed set of photon energies means the atom can change its energy only by fixed amounts, the differences between a fixed set of allowed levels.

questions.q: In a sodium atom, an electron makes a transition from an energy level at −3.03 eV to one at −5.14 eV. What is the frequency of the emitted photon? Take h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
optionWhy: A student who takes the photon energy as the energy of the starting level uses 3.03 eV and gets 7.31 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The photon carries the difference between the two levels, 2.11 eV.
A student who adds the sizes of the two negative levels uses 3.03 + 5.14 = 8.17 eV and gets 1.97 × 10¹⁵ Hz. The difference is (−3.03) − (−5.14) = 2.11 eV.
A student who puts 2.11 eV straight into f = E/h without converting to joules gets 3.18 × 10³³ Hz. h is in J s, so the energy must be in joules: 2.11 eV = 3.38 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

questions.q: Two discharge tubes, P and Q, each contain a single gas. The emission spectrum of each gas shows exactly four bright lines in the visible region, but none of the wavelengths of the lines from P matches any of the wavelengths of the lines from Q. A student claims that P and Q contain the same element. Which statement is correct?
options: The claim is correct, because the number of lines is set by the number of electrons in an atom of the element.
P and Q may contain the same element, because a gas at a higher temperature emits its lines at shorter wavelengths.
The claim is wrong, because an element is identified by the wavelengths of its lines, and none match.
The claim is correct if the two tubes glow with the same overall colour, since that colour identifies an element.
optionWhy: A student who counts lines as electrons picks this. Lines come from transitions between energy levels, and one electron can make many transitions, so the number of lines does not identify an element; the wavelengths do, and here none of them match.

A student who transfers 'hotter means bluer' from a glowing solid to a gas picks this. The line wavelengths are fixed by the atom's energy levels and do not shift with temperature, so lines at different wavelengths mean different elements.

Each element has its own set of energy levels, so the wavelengths of its lines form a unique pattern. Two gases whose lines share no wavelength cannot be the same element, however many lines each shows.

A student who identifies elements by the blended colour of the glow picks this. The eye merges the lines into one colour, and different elements can look alike; the spectrometer shows that no line wavelengths coincide, so the gases are different elements.
questions.explain: Each element has its own set of energy levels, so the wavelengths of its lines form a unique pattern. Two gases whose lines share no wavelength cannot be the same element, however many lines each shows.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the binding energy of a nucleus?
options: The energy released when the nucleus is separated completely into its nucleons.
The energy stored inside the nucleus, which it gives out when it later decays.
The minimum energy needed to pull the nucleus apart into separate nucleons.
The energy equivalent of the extra mass a nucleus has over its separate nucleons.
optionWhy: A student who thinks that breaking bonds releases energy picks this. The direction is reversed: energy is released when a nucleus forms from separate nucleons, and the same amount must be supplied to separate them.

A student who pictures binding energy as a store held by the nucleus picks this. Binding energy is the energy needed to take the nucleus apart; a more tightly bound nucleus has less mass-energy than its separated nucleons, not more.
Nucleons attract one another through the strong nuclear force, so energy must be supplied to pull them apart. The binding energy is this energy; it equals the mass defect multiplied by c².
A student who thinks binding adds mass picks this. A nucleus has LESS mass than its separated nucleons; the binding energy is the energy equivalent of this mass defect.
questions.explain: Nucleons attract one another through the strong nuclear force, so energy must be supplied to pull them apart. The binding energy is this energy; it equals the mass defect multiplied by c².

questions.q: Radium-226 decays by α emission: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α. The atomic masses are 226.025410 u for radium-226, 222.017578 u for radon-222 and 4.002603 u for helium-4 (the electron masses cancel). Take 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻², 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. How much energy is released in the decay of one radium-226 nucleus?
optionWhy: A student who multiplies the mass by c instead of c² gets 8.685 × 10⁻³⁰ × 3.00 × 10⁸ = 2.6 × 10⁻²¹. Its unit would be kg m s⁻¹, which is not an energy; E = mc² needs c² = 9.00 × 10¹⁶ m² s⁻².

A student who takes the mass converted to be the α particle's mass gets 4.002603 × 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg × c² = 6.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ J. The α particle is emitted, not destroyed; only the 0.005229 u decrease in total mass becomes energy.
A student who finds 0.005229 × 931.5 = 4.87 MeV and converts it with 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J gets 7.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. That factor converts eV; 1 MeV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹³ J, so 4.87 MeV = 7.8 × 10⁻¹³ J.

questions.q: Nucleons in a nucleus are about 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, while the nuclei of neighbouring atoms in a solid are about 10⁻¹⁰ m apart. Why does the strong nuclear force bind the nucleons within each nucleus but have no effect between neighbouring nuclei?
options: Its range is so short that it is negligible at separations much above 10⁻¹⁵ m.
It is a repulsive force between nuclei, as every nucleus carries positive charge.
The electrons around each nucleus block the force from reaching other nuclei.
It falls as 1/r², so at 10⁻¹⁰ m it is 10¹⁰ times weaker than it is inside a nucleus.
optionWhy: The strong force is short-range: very strong between nucleons about 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, but negligible a few times further out. Nuclei in a solid are about 10⁵ times further apart than that, so they do not feel it.

A student who thinks the strong force depends on charge picks this. The strong force attracts nucleons whatever their charge; the repulsion between nuclei is the ELECTRIC force. The strong force is absent between nuclei because of its short range.
A student who thinks material in the way can block a force picks this. Nothing shields the strong force; it simply does not extend beyond a few times 10⁻¹⁵ m.

A student who assumes every force follows an inverse-square law picks this. If the strong force fell as 1/r², it would fall in step with the electric force and stay stronger than the repulsion between nuclei, so nuclei in a solid would be pulled together. The strong force falls off far faster than 1/r².
questions.explain: The strong force is short-range: very strong between nucleons about 10⁻¹⁵ m apart, but negligible a few times further out. Nuclei in a solid are about 10⁵ times further apart than that, so they do not feel it.
questions.working: The strong nuclear force acts only over distances of the order of 10⁻¹⁵ m. Neighbouring nuclei in a solid are about 10⁻¹⁰ m apart, 10⁵ times further, where the strong force is negligible.

questions.q: A nucleus X undergoes α decay. The daughter nucleus then undergoes two β⁻ decays in succession. How does the final nucleus compare with X?
options: It is an isotope of X whose nucleus has six fewer neutrons than X.
It is another element, with two fewer protons and two fewer neutrons.
It is another element, with four fewer protons and as many neutrons as X.
It is an isotope of X whose nucleus has four fewer neutrons than X.
optionWhy: A student who thinks each β particle carries away a nucleon subtracts two more from A, giving N − 6. A β particle is an electron with nucleon number 0: in β⁻ decay A is unchanged while one neutron becomes a proton.

A student who thinks β⁻ particles come from the electron shells leaves the nucleus unchanged after the α decay. β⁻ particles come from the nucleus: each one raises Z by 1, returning the nucleus to the element X.

A student who thinks β⁻ decay turns a proton into a neutron lowers Z by a further 2 and restores the 2 neutrons. It is the other way round: β⁻ decay turns a neutron into a proton, making the nucleus more positive, as charge conservation requires.

α decay removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons; each β⁻ decay turns a neutron into a proton. Overall Z is unchanged (−2 + 1 + 1) and N falls by 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, so the result is an isotope of X with a nucleon number 4 less.
questions.explain: α decay removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons; each β⁻ decay turns a neutron into a proton. Overall Z is unchanged (−2 + 1 + 1) and N falls by 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, so the result is an isotope of X with a nucleon number 4 less.
questions.working: α decay: Z − 2, N − 2 (A − 4). Each β⁻ decay: a neutron becomes a proton, so Z + 1 and N − 1 (A unchanged). Overall: Z − 2 + 1 + 1 = Z (same element); N − 2 − 1 − 1 = N − 4; A − 4. The final nucleus is an isotope of X with 4 fewer neutrons.

questions.q: Which of these radioactive decay equations is correct?
options: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν
¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₁₀Ne + ⁰₊₁e + ⁰₀ν
²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α
¹³⁷ᵐ₅₆Ba → ¹³⁷₅₅Cs + γ
optionWhy: A student who pairs the positron with the antineutrino, and so the electron with the neutrino, picks this. β⁻ decay emits an electron and an electron ANTINEUTRINO: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ⁰₀ν̄.
A student who thinks β⁺ decay turns a neutron into a proton raises Z to 10. Charge is then not conserved (9 ≠ 10 + 1). In β⁺ decay a proton becomes a neutron: ¹⁸₉F → ¹⁸₈O + ⁰₊₁e + ⁰₀ν.
Nucleon number: 226 = 222 + 4. Charge: 88 = 86 + 2. An α particle is a helium-4 nucleus, so radium (Z = 88) becomes radon (Z = 86).

A student who thinks γ emission changes the element lowers Z. A γ photon has no charge and no nucleon number, so charge would not balance (56 ≠ 55). The excited barium-137m nucleus becomes ¹³⁷₅₆Ba in its ground state.
questions.explain: Nucleon number: 226 = 222 + 4. Charge: 88 = 86 + 2. An α particle is a helium-4 nucleus, so radium (Z = 88) becomes radon (Z = 86).
questions.working: Check each equation for conservation of nucleon number and charge, and for the right particles. α: 226 = 222 + 4 and 88 = 86 + 2, correct. β⁻ (carbon-14): the numbers balance, but β⁻ decay emits an antineutrino, ⁰₀ν̄, not a neutrino. β⁺ (fluorine-18): charge 9 ≠ 10 + 1; the daughter is ¹⁸₈O. γ: charge 56 ≠ 55 + 0; γ emission leaves the nuclide as ¹³⁷₅₆Ba.

questions.q: An electron antineutrino, ν̄, is emitted in every β⁻ decay. Which statement about the antineutrino is correct?
options: It is a neutron that leaves the nucleus together with the β⁻ particle.
It is uncharged, has a very small mass and very rarely interacts with matter.
It is positively charged, balancing the negative charge of the β⁻ particle.
It is a high-energy photon, emitted as the new nucleus loses energy.
optionWhy: A student who confuses the similar names picks this. In β⁻ decay a neutron is used up, not emitted: it becomes a proton. The antineutrino has nucleon number 0 (⁰₀ν̄).
Antineutrinos, like neutrinos, have zero charge and a mass far smaller than the electron's, and they interact so rarely that almost all of them pass straight through the Earth.
A student who takes 'anti' to mean 'opposite charge' picks this. Charge balances without it: a neutron (0) becomes a proton (+1) and an electron (−1). The antineutrino is uncharged.

A student who merges the antineutrino with the γ photon picks this. A γ photon comes from an excited nucleus dropping to a lower energy state; the antineutrino is a separate particle created in β⁻ decay.
questions.explain: Antineutrinos, like neutrinos, have zero charge and a mass far smaller than the electron's, and they interact so rarely that almost all of them pass straight through the Earth.

questions.q: Technetium-99m emits γ rays only and has a half-life of 6.0 h. It is injected into patients so that the organs that take it up can be imaged by a γ camera outside the body. Which statement is a correct reason for choosing technetium-99m?
options: Its γ rays are strongly ionizing, so they give a strong signal at the camera.
Its half-life is short because so little is injected, and a small sample halves quickly.
Its γ rays make the organ's own tissue radioactive, so that the organ shows up.
Its γ rays are weakly ionizing and most pass out of the body to the camera.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the most penetrating radiation is also the most ionizing picks this. γ rays are the least ionizing radiation, which is why they escape the body; strongly ionizing α particles would be absorbed within it.

A student who thinks half-life depends on the amount of material picks this. Half-life is a property of the nuclide: technetium-99m has a half-life of 6.0 h whether the sample is a trace or a large quantity.
A student who thinks irradiation makes things radioactive picks this. γ rays do not make tissue radioactive; the organ shows up because the technetium-99m itself collects there and emits γ rays.

γ rays are the most penetrating and least ionizing radiation, so most pass out of the body to the camera and relatively little energy is deposited in the patient. The short half-life then limits the dose after the scan.
questions.explain: γ rays are the most penetrating and least ionizing radiation, so most pass out of the body to the camera and relatively little energy is deposited in the patient. The short half-life then limits the dose after the scan.

questions.q: A hospital prepares a dose of technetium-99m (half-life 6.0 h) that has an activity of 800 MBq at 08:00. What will its activity be at 14:00 the next day?
options: 0 MBq
160 MBq
25 MBq
12.5 MBq
optionWhy: A student who thinks half-life is half the time to decay completely expects all the technetium-99m to have gone after 12 h. In fact the activity halves every 6.0 h and is still 25 MBq after 30 h.
A student who divides by the number of half-lives gets 800/5 = 160 MBq. Five half-lives divide the activity by 2⁵ = 32.
From 08:00 to 14:00 the next day is 30 h, which is five half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 MBq.
A student who counts the six clock times 08:00, 14:00, 20:00, 02:00, 08:00 and 14:00 as six half-lives halves six times, giving 12.5 MBq. Those six times enclose only five 6-hour intervals.
questions.explain: From 08:00 to 14:00 the next day is 30 h, which is five half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 → 50 → 25 MBq.
questions.working: From 08:00 to 14:00 the next day is 30 h = 30 h/6.0 h = 5 half-lives. A = 800 MBq × (½)⁵ = 800 MBq/32 = 25 MBq.

questions.q: With no radioactive source near it, a detector still records a count rate. Which statement about this background count rate is correct?
options: It is the same in every minute, so a single one-minute reading gives its value exactly and no repeat readings are needed.
It is radiation that has soaked into the detector from sources used earlier, and it fades once the detector is left unused.
It comes from cosmic rays and from radioactive nuclides in rock, air and buildings and is subtracted from each reading.
It needs to be subtracted only from the first reading taken with a source; later readings then show the source alone.
optionWhy: A student who thinks of background as a steady value picks this. Background counts come from random decays and random cosmic-ray arrivals, so they fluctuate from minute to minute; a reliable value needs a long counting time or the average of several readings.

A student who thinks radiation can be stored in an object picks this. Radiation is not a substance that collects in a detector; the background is present in any new detector, anywhere, because cosmic rays and natural radioactive nuclides surround us.

Background radiation arrives from cosmic rays and from natural radioactive nuclides (for example radon in the air and potassium-40 in rocks and buildings). A detector records it whether or not a source is present, so it is measured separately and subtracted from each reading to give the source's corrected count rate.

A student who thinks subtraction 'removes' the background from the detector picks this. The detector goes on recording background in every reading; the subtraction is a correction the experimenter applies to each reading, not a change to the detector.
questions.explain: Background radiation arrives from cosmic rays and from natural radioactive nuclides (for example radon in the air and potassium-40 in rocks and buildings). A detector records it whether or not a source is present, so it is measured separately and subtracted from each reading to give the source's corrected count rate.

questions.q: A chain reaction of uranium-235 fission in a reactor core is proceeding at a steady rate. Which condition is being met?
options: On average, exactly one of the neutrons from each fission causes a further fission.
Each fission releases exactly one neutron, which goes on to cause a further fission.
The fission fragments split again in turn, each one releasing further neutrons.
The moderator absorbs the surplus neutrons, leaving one per fission to continue the chain.
optionWhy: Some neutrons escape and some are absorbed without causing fission. If on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another fission, every generation has the same number of fissions and the rate is steady.

A student who thinks every neutron released goes on to cause a fission reasons that a steady rate needs exactly one neutron per fission. A fission of uranium-235 releases two or three neutrons, about 2.4 on average; the rate is steady because, on average, all but one of them escape or are absorbed without causing fission.

A student who thinks the chain consists of fragments splitting again picks this. Fragments such as barium and krypton do not undergo fission; they decay by β⁻ emission. The chain is carried by the neutrons.

A student who reads 'moderate' as 'keep under control' picks this. A moderator slows neutrons and must absorb as few as possible; the surplus neutrons escape from the core or are absorbed without causing fission, for example by the control rods.
questions.explain: Some neutrons escape and some are absorbed without causing fission. If on average exactly one neutron from each fission causes another fission, every generation has the same number of fissions and the rate is steady.

questions.q: A fission of uranium-235 produces barium-141 (¹⁴¹₅₆Ba) and krypton-92 (⁹²₃₆Kr). The heaviest stable isotopes of these elements are barium-138 (¹³⁸₅₆Ba) and krypton-86 (⁸⁶₃₆Kr). Which decay are barium-141 and krypton-92 expected to undergo?
options: β⁺ decay, which converts a surplus neutron into a proton
α decay, which carries the surplus neutrons away
β⁻ decay, which turns a surplus neutron into a proton
γ decay only, as nuclei formed by fission are stable
optionWhy: A student who has the two β decays the wrong way round picks this. In β⁺ decay a proton changes into a neutron, which would make the neutron excess worse; the neutron-to-proton change needs β⁻ decay.

A student who thinks α decay removes excess neutrons picks this. An α particle removes two protons and two neutrons, which does not reduce the neutron excess of these fragments; they decay by β⁻ emission.

Barium-141 has 85 neutrons against at most 82 in stable barium, and krypton-92 has 56 against at most 50. In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton, reducing the neutron excess; both nuclides are β⁻ emitters.

A student who thinks fission products are ordinary stable nuclei picks this. Both fragments have more neutrons than any stable isotope of their element, so they are radioactive and decay by β⁻ emission.
questions.explain: Barium-141 has 85 neutrons against at most 82 in stable barium, and krypton-92 has 56 against at most 50. In β⁻ decay a neutron changes into a proton, reducing the neutron excess; both nuclides are β⁻ emitters.
questions.working: Barium-141 has N = 141 − 56 = 85 neutrons; stable barium has at most 138 − 56 = 82. Krypton-92 has N = 92 − 36 = 56; stable krypton has at most 86 − 36 = 50. Both fragments have surplus neutrons, so they undergo β⁻ decay, in which a neutron changes into a proton (Z increases by 1, N decreases by 1).

questions.q: A main-sequence star stays the same size for millions of years. Which statement explains why it does not collapse?
options: Its rotation produces an outward centrifugal force on its gas that balances the inward pull of gravity.
No forces act on its gas at all, which is why the star is neither expanding nor contracting.
The inward gravitational forces on its gas are balanced by the outward radiation pressure maintained by fusion.
Gravity is negligible in space, so the hot gas of the star has no weight that needs supporting.
optionWhy: A student who treats centrifugal force as a real outward force picks this. A star does not need to rotate to be stable, and the Sun rotates far too slowly for this to matter; the outward support comes from pressure maintained by fusion.

A student who thinks equilibrium means 'no forces' picks this. Enormous forces act: gravity pulls every layer inwards. The star keeps its size because the outward pressure balances gravity, so the resultant force is zero.

In a stable star the inward gravitational force on each layer is balanced by the outward pressure maintained by the energy released in fusion in the core. The forces are large; it is their balance that keeps the size constant.
A student who believes there is no gravity in space picks this. A star's own mass produces a huge gravitational field; without the outward pressure maintained by fusion the star would collapse.
questions.explain: In a stable star the inward gravitational force on each layer is balanced by the outward pressure maintained by the energy released in fusion in the core. The forces are large; it is their balance that keeps the size constant.

questions.q: Hydrogen fusion in a star needs a core temperature of the order of 10⁷ K. Why is such a high temperature needed?
options: Fusion absorbs energy, and the thermal energy of the core supplies it.
Hydrogen must reach its ignition temperature before it can burn.
Nuclei need enough energy to overcome the strong nuclear force.
Nuclei must move fast enough to overcome electric repulsion.
optionWhy: A student who assumes a reaction that needs heat must absorb energy picks this. Each fusion reaction releases far more energy than the colliding nuclei needed; the high temperature only gets them close enough to fuse.

A student who thinks stars burn like a fire picks this. Nothing burns in a star's core: there is no combustion, and chemical reactions could not supply a star's energy. The temperature is needed for nuclear fusion.

A student who thinks the strong force is the barrier picks this. The strong nuclear force is attractive and short-range; it is what binds the nuclei once they are close. The barrier is their electric repulsion.
Nuclei are positively charged and repel. Only at very high temperatures do enough nuclei move fast enough to approach within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, where the attractive strong nuclear force can bind them.
questions.explain: Nuclei are positively charged and repel. Only at very high temperatures do enough nuclei move fast enough to approach within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, where the attractive strong nuclear force can bind them.

questions.q: Which sequence of stages describes the evolution of a star of 1 M⊙, such as the Sun, after it forms?
options: Main sequence → red giant → supernova explosion
Main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
Main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → black hole
Main sequence → white dwarf → red giant → red supergiant
optionWhy: A student who thinks every star explodes when its fuel runs out picks this. Only stars of high initial mass (more than about 8 M⊙) end as supernovae. A star of 1 M⊙ becomes a red giant, sheds its outer layers gently as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf.

When core hydrogen is used up, a 1 M⊙ star swells into a red giant. Its core never gets hot enough for fusion beyond carbon and oxygen; the outer layers are shed as a planetary nebula and the exposed core becomes a white dwarf.

A student who thinks all stars end as black holes picks this. Only the cores of the most massive stars become black holes, after a supernova; a 1 M⊙ star sheds a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf.

A student who thinks stars grow as they age, from dwarfs into giants, picks this. The white dwarf is the LAST stage: it is the exposed core left after the red-giant stage, and no fusion takes place in it. A star of 1 M⊙ never becomes a supergiant.
questions.explain: When core hydrogen is used up, a 1 M⊙ star swells into a red giant. Its core never gets hot enough for fusion beyond carbon and oxygen; the outer layers are shed as a planetary nebula and the exposed core becomes a white dwarf.

questions.q: Two measurements of the position of a nearby star against very distant background stars, made six months apart, differ by an angle of 0.0700 arc-second. Take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m and 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. What is the distance to the star in AU?
optionWhy: A student who uses the whole 0.0700 arc-second shift as the parallax angle gets d = 14.3 pc = 2.94 × 10⁶ AU, half the true distance. The parallax angle is half the shift between observations six months apart.
A student who treats d = 1/p as giving light-years takes 28.6 ly = 2.70 × 10¹⁷ m = 1.80 × 10⁶ AU. With p in arc-seconds, 1/p gives parsecs, and a parsec is 3.26 ly.
A student who takes the distance as proportional to the parallax angle uses d = 0.0350 pc and gets 7.21 × 10³ AU. Distance is the reciprocal: d = 1/p = 28.6 pc.
